To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the interhemispheric transfer of information is an adaptive mechanism, which changes dynamically in response to the complexity of the task, and which allows the optimal allocation of information processing between the two hemispheres.

(1) the interhemispheric transfer is an important component of cognitive functioning; (2) it is a flexible system that can be modulated by task demands and cognitive abilities; (3) the interhemisphere coupling is a mechanism that can be used to compensate for the decline in the efficiency of monohemisphere processing systems; (4) the decline in the ability to use the interhemispherically coupled processing in Alzheimer's disease may contribute to the cognitive decline in this disease
the adaptive nature of the inter-hemispheric system is crucial in maintaining cognitive abilities during normal ageing and in Alzheimer's disease (AD).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of interhemispheric transfer in the maintenance of cognitive functions with aging, and its disruption in Alzheimer's disease.
the role of the corpus callosum in the development of cognitive skills in normal ageing, and in the development of dementia.
understanding the functional organization of the human brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the corpus callosum plays a key role in the maintenance and compensation of cognitive functions with aging and that the failure of its function in Alzheimer's disease could explain some of the cognitive deficits in this pathology.
the role of inter-hemispheric coupling is not well understood in the normal ageing brain, but it may play a role in the maintenance of cognitive functions in normal ageing.

there is no conclusive evidence for the presence of interhemispheric asymmetries in the normal aging brain and no evidence for the presence and role of interhemispheric asymmetries in Alzheimer's Disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the adaptive nature of the interhemispheric transfer of information is a key factor in maintaining the integrity of cognitive functions in normal aging, whereas in Alzheimer disease the interhemispherical coupling is impaired, and the cognitive decline cannot be compensated by interhemispheric mechanisms.
, in healthy aging, the brain is able to compensate for age-related declines by using adaptive mechanisms that allow it to optimally distribute the processing demands across hemispheres.

the adaptive nature of brain function and its underlying mechanisms, such as interhemispheric interactions, may not be able to compensate for the loss of cognitive abilities in Alzheimer's disease (AD).
The main takeaway from our work is that

the brain's capacity to flexibly adjust its interhemispheric interactions in order to optimize the processing of information may underlie the recent findings of age-related changes in cerebral lateralization.
the brain is a flexible system that is able to reorganize itself in order to compensate for the effects of brain damage.
the interhemispheric transfer of information is not a fixed process.
